lessons.title: ఉదయం (udayam) — the same Sanskrit root, a different job than in Kannada
lessons.gloss: "morning" (udayam) — Sanskrit tatsama from udaya ("rise") + Telugu -mu, Telugu's most general everyday word, though genuine native competitors (poddu/podduna, vēkuva) also do real everyday work; unlike Kannada, where the same Sanskrit root (udaya) shows up ONLY inside the greeting śubhōdaya, Telugu's everyday noun and its greeting-root are the SAME word

segments.text: Last lesson's రోజు was a genuine Persian surprise. This lesson's word for "morning" goes the other way — straight Sanskrit, doing double duty in a way its Kannada cousin doesn't.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - ఉదయం — Sanskrit, and genuinely everyday

segments.text: ఉదయం (udayam) — "morning" — is a Sanskrit tatsama: from ఉదయ (udaya, "rise, appearance") plus Telugu's own -ము (-mu) nominal suffix. This is Telugu's most common, general everyday word for "morning" — but be honest: it doesn't have the field entirely to itself. పొద్దు/పొద్దున (poddu/podduna) is genuine Proto-Dravidian vocabulary — cognate with Tamil pozhudu and Kannada hottu — and does real everyday work too ("పొద్దున్నే లేచాను," "I woke up in the morning"). వేకువ (vēkuva, "dawn, early morning") is labeled colloquial, not archaic or purely poetic. ఉదయం is the broadest, most general word — but not an uncontested one.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way: Be honest: the same root, doing a different job than in Kannada

segments.text: Here's the honest cross-language twist. Kannada also has this exact Sanskrit root, ఉదయ (udaya) — but only inside its greeting, ಶುಭೋದಯ (śubhōdaya, "good morning"). Kannada's actual everyday noun for "morning" is a completely unrelated native word, ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ (beḷagge, "the shining"). Telugu doesn't split the job that way: ఉదయం (udayam) covers both the everyday noun AND, in శుభోదయం, the greeting root — one word, doing what Kannada spreads across two unrelated ones. And unlike రోజు (last lesson's genuine Persian surprise for "day"), Telugu's morning word holds no such twist — straightforwardly Sanskrit, start to finish.

segments.text: Is ఉదయం (udayam) the ONLY word Telugu speakers use for "morning"? (No — it's the broadest, most common one, but పొద్దు/పొద్దున and వేకువ, both genuinely native, do real everyday work too.) Does Kannada's everyday morning-noun share ఉదయం (udayam)'s root? (No — Kannada's ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ is native; the shared root, udaya, shows up only inside Kannada's GREETING, ಶುಭೋದಯ.) Does ఉదయం (udayam) hold a surprise the way రోజు did? (No — straightforwardly Sanskrit throughout.)

lessons.title: ఋ (ṛ) — one character, met inside a word you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ఋ — recognised inside a word you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ఋ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: భ — what does it do? And one from further back: ఎ?
One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
It is an independent vowel — the shape a vowel takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside a word. You have met that pairing twice already, at ఉ and at ఎ.

What makes this one worth a page of its own is what the vowel is. It is an r doing a vowel's work: a whole syllable with no other vowel in it, the way English lets l carry the second half of bottle. Telugu took the letter from Sanskrit along with the words that need it, and modern speakers give it the sound ru.
You already say this one, and it has ఋ (ṛ) at the front of its second word:
వసంత ఋతువు vasanta ṛtuvu — the spring season.
ఋ (ṛ) is one of the rarest letters in the alphabet: outside Sanskrit borrowings it has almost nowhere to appear. Meeting it once, on a word you can already say, is enough for now.

blocks.title: Writing: ఋ — copy what you see

segments.text: Put your pen on ఋ (ṛ) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

segments.text: Which character is this — ఋ (ṛ)? What kind of thing is it — a consonant, a vowel sign, or an independent vowel? (An independent vowel, sounded ru.) Name the word you already say that contains it.
